slides.title: Rectifiability: geometry visible to measure
slides.notes: Open the lecture by making rectifiability a promise about visibility. We are not saying that a set is smooth everywhere. We are saying that, after discarding negligible leftovers, the set can be inspected through countably many Lipschitz pieces with stable densities and almost everywhere tangent planes.

slides.title: Three tests for a geometric set
slides.notes: Use this slide to set the working standard for the rest of the deck. The chapter vocabulary can feel encyclopedic, so compress it into three recurring questions: which charts cover the mass, what the microscope sees almost everywhere, and whether oriented pieces leave the right boundary.

slides.title: Rectifiable means countably charted, not smooth
slides.notes: Emphasize that the word countable does real work. A rectifiable set may have many pieces, seams, corners, and a negligible remainder. What it cannot have, in positive m-dimensional measure, is geometry that refuses all Lipschitz chart descriptions at the scale being measured.

slides.title: The first local test is mass growth
slides.notes: Treat density as the first microscope before discussing tangent planes. Students often try to recognize a smooth curve by eye, but the measure-theoretic test asks how mass grows inside shrinking balls. Stable normalized growth is the quantitative hint that an m-dimensional object is present.

slides.title: Approximate tangents are limiting flat pictures
slides.notes: Connect this to the density slide. Density says the right amount of mass is present; the tangent test asks whether that mass has a coherent direction. The qualifier approximate matters because isolated bad samples and negligible seams do not control the almost-everywhere geometry of the set.

slides.title: Lipschitz images carry mass through Jacobians
slides.notes: Present this as the computational bridge rather than a theorem to memorize. If the set is built from Lipschitz charts, then m-dimensional mass should be computable by changing variables on those charts. The Jacobian measures stretching, and the multiplicity term prevents folded sheets from being undercounted.

slides.title: Good shadows can certify visible geometry
slides.notes: Use projections to give students a second kind of evidence. A rectifiable set is not merely large; it casts shadows in ways compatible with tangent planes and area. The contrasting dust picture is deliberately schematic, showing why positive measure alone does not force rectifiability.

slides.title: Orientation turns a rectifiable set into a tester
slides.notes: This is the conceptual handoff from rectifiable sets to homological integration language. The set supplies the support, but the current is an operator: it eats a test form and returns a number. Orientation and multiplicity are the extra data that make boundary algebra possible.

slides.title: Cancellation is the algebra behind gluing
slides.notes: Slow down on this slide because it makes the current language tangible. The boundary operator is not an extra decoration; it records whether the oriented geometry was assembled consistently. If an internal edge remains after gluing, the algebra has detected a real geometric defect.

slides.title: From visual story to finite check
slides.notes: Tie the formal material back to the assigned notebook. The artifact check is intentionally small, but its discipline is excellent: name the object, name the allowed perturbation, name the invariant, and explain which hypothesis would make the conclusion fail if removed.

slides.title: How the chapter's theorems fit together
slides.notes: This slide is the instructor map. Instead of walking through every theorem in isolation, show how the chapter repeatedly turns hypotheses into permissions. The proof habit is to ask what operation becomes legal, what quantity becomes measurable, and which example would break the statement without that permission.

slides.title: Classify the evidence, not the drawing
slides.notes: This exercise prevents passive recognition. Students should not answer that the blue part looks nice and the orange part looks bad. They should cite a chart cover, a density prediction, a tangent-plane prediction, or a current boundary rule, then say which hypothesis keeps that evidence legitimate.

slides.title: Rectifiability is the bridge from rough sets to calculus
slides.notes: Close by returning to the promise from the title slide. Rectifiability does not make every set smooth; it makes enough of the set charted, measurable, tangent-bearing, and orientable that calculus and boundary algebra can be performed without pretending the geometry is globally regular.
